To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the most effective hand hygiene campaigns are those that include all the components of a comprehensive hand hygiene programme, and that these campaigns are more likely to be successful when they are led by a multidisciplinary team, and supported by the institution's senior leadership.

the successful hand hygiene promotion programme was a multifaceted intervention that included: (1) the use of alcohol-based hand rub (ABHR) instead of soap and water; (2) a multimodal strategy to change the hand hygiene behaviour of healthcare workers; (3) an organisational culture change that supported the intervention; (4) the involvement of senior leadership; (5) a strong focus on education and feedback; (6) the use of a multidisciplinary team; (7)

a comprehensive, multimodal hand hygiene promotion programme that includes a focus on the institutional culture, a strong institutional commitment, and the use of a variety of educational and quality improvement strategies can lead to a dramatic improvement in hand hygiene compliance and a reduction in healthcare-associated infection.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether a multimodal approach to hand hygiene promotion can be successfully implemented in a large tertiary hospital in the UK.
the question of how to improve hand hygiene compliance and reduce healthcare-associated infections.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
they did it by being thorough, systematic, and persistent, and by having a strong, supportive and committed team.

the Kirkland et al1 programme was successful because it: was led by the infection control team and was supported by the hospital leadership; involved a multifaceted approach to hand hygiene promotion, including the provision of alcohol-based hand rubs (ABHRs) and the development and implementation of a hand hygiene campaign; and included an ongoing evaluation and monitoring of hand hygiene compliance, which was used to guide the programme.
Kirkland et al1 were successful because they had an effective and sustained programme of hand hygiene promotion that involved a number of key components.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we need to ‘think big, think simple, act fast and act now’.

the Kirkland et al programme had a strong evidence base, was multifaceted, and had strong leadership support.3 The evidence base for their programme included a review of the literature,4 a review of the current situation at their hospital, and a baseline hand hygiene compliance audit.
The main takeaway from our work is that

it is important for infection control practitioners to be aware of the importance of organisational culture change in order to achieve a sustained increase in hand hygiene and a reduction in healthcare-associated infection rates.
the Kirkland team were able to make significant improvements to hand hygiene and reduce hospital-acquired infection rates through a combination of multifaceted, multimodal interventions.
a multifaceted approach to hand hygiene promotion is necessary, but not sufficient.
